newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Churches hit Nigeria, Shell over Ogoni violence.
newsitem.headline: Churches hit Nigeria, Shell over Ogoni violence.

text.p: The World Council of Churches (WCC) has accused Nigeria's military regime of widespread oppression in oil-rich Ogoniland and attacked the Shell oil company for causing environmental devastation in the region.

The accusations were made in a 106-page report compiled by the Geneva-based WCC and issued on Monday after a visit last year to Nigeria -- which executed nine Ogoni leaders in December 1995 -- by a senior WCC official, Deborah Robinson.

"A quiet state of siege prevails even today on Ogoniland. Intimidation, rape, arrests, torture, shooting and looting by the soldiers continues to occur," declared the report, "Ogoni: The Struggle Continues."

It argued that Shell which operates in Nigeria through a subsidiary which it says halted operations in Ogoniland in 1993 because of intimidation by Ogoni activists, had been justifiably criticised for its operations in the region.
"It is no wonder why Shell has been the target of international sanctions: its environmental record in Ogoniland and in other minority oil-producing areas is distasteful," the WCC report declared.
A Shell spokesman in London said the company would not comment until it had details of the report's allegations.
"The World Council of Churches has not asked us for comment and we think it would be premature for us to say anything else until we see the report," said spokesman Eric Nickson.

Robinson went to Ogoniland in the wake of the execution of Ogoni activist and writer Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other campaigners for local rights who were accused by the government of instigating the murder of four Ogoni chiefs.
The hangings, after a brief trial, brought widespread international criticism of Nigeria's military government.

Saro-Wiwa had himself campaigned for compensation from Shell for damage he and his supporters said its Nigerian subsidiary, the Shell Petroleum Development Company (SPDC) had done to the environment through careless exploitation of oil reserves.

For several years Shell, one of the world's largest businesses, has countered the criticism through advertisements arguing that its presence had helped development of the region and of Nigeria as a whole.
But the report from the WCC, which links more than 330 churches in over 100 countries, rejected this assertion.

The company, it said, was not working in the interests of the local people "because not only do the Ogoni not benefit from the oil industry, (but) they have suffered the brunt of environmental devastation, military repression and judicial as well as extra-judicial murder."

In an introduction to the report, WCC executive director Dr Samuel Kobia said the body's concern was for all the people of Nigeria although the report focussed on the Ogoni "to highlight a socio-political malaise that is generally widespread."
"Many Nigerians, and especially the churches, are desirous that the truth about the situation in their country be made known to the outside world," Kobia wrote.

The document called on the Nigerian authorities for the restoration of democracy, the liberation of 19 other Ogoni activists in detention and the release for proper burial of the bodies of Saro-Wiwa and his executed colleagues.
It also urged Shell to clean up existing oil spills and to use its own influence with the Lagos government to ensure protection of human rights in the country.
